lesson.title: A War on Poverty: The Great Society's Sweeping Reforms
lesson.summary: Lyndon Johnson's Great Society was a broad set of programs in the mid-1960s aimed at eliminating poverty, expanding civil rights, and improving education, health care, and the environment, making it one of the most ambitious reform agendas since the New Deal.
lesson.body:
President Johnson introduced his vision in a speech at the University of Michigan on May 22, 1964, describing a "Great Society" that would go beyond material abundance to also address poverty, injustice, and quality of life. Coming on the heels of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, this agenda extended the principle of equal opportunity from the law itself into economic and social policy more broadly.

The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 launched what Johnson called the "War on Poverty," creating the Office of Economic Opportunity and a set of programs that included Job Corps, offering job training for young people, VISTA, a domestic counterpart to the Peace Corps, and Community Action Programs that funneled federal money directly to local anti-poverty efforts. Head Start, the early childhood education program for children from low-income families, soon followed as one of the War on Poverty's most enduring initiatives.

The year 1965 alone saw a remarkable wave of legislation. Medicare and Medicaid extended health coverage to the elderly and to many low-income Americans. The Elementary and Secondary Education Act sent federal funding to schools serving low-income students at a scale not attempted before. The Higher Education Act expanded college financial aid. The Immigration and Nationality Act overhauled the nation's immigration law. And the Department of Housing and Urban Development was established as a new cabinet agency.

The Great Society also included consumer protection and environmental measures, such as auto safety standards and early clean air and water laws, funding for the arts and humanities through newly created National Endowments, and the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, which established public television and radio in the United States.

Many of these programs endured. Medicare, Medicaid, and Head Start remain central parts of the American social safety net today. But the Great Society's broader ambitions were curtailed as the Vietnam War drained federal budgets and political attention in the later 1960s, leaving behind a legacy that mixes lasting achievement with unfinished promise.
